vignette: After six sessions, I have learned to read the map of her days, but the timeline begins two years ago, on a Tuesday, while she is kneeling in a client's basement. One moment she is tightening a fitting; the next, her abdomen caves inward, and a white-hot wave drags her to the floor. The ambulance ride is a blur of shouting and spinning ceiling lights. She wakes in an ICU bed with a breathing tube in her throat and leather restraints holding her wrists. Her appendix had perforated, triggering sepsis. Her heart stops at 3:14 a.m. They bring her back with a charged paddle and a litany of vasopressors. She remembers the cold, the relentless beeping, the way the nurses' voices sound like they are speaking through water. When they finally remove the tube, she swallows glass. Her body was supposed to keep her safe. Now it is a traitor. She spends the next two years rebuilding muscle and nerve. Her family in Lahore calls daily, but she answers less often, telling them over the crackling line that she is fine, that the surgeon is excellent, that work will wait. She is forty-five, unmarried, and accustomed to doing things alone, but this recovery forces a dependency she resents. Physical therapy burns; occupational therapy teaches her to lift with her legs, not her back. When she finally returns to the pipe yard, she clips her tool belt with a mechanical click that sounds too much like a code alarm. Her hands, which once read pipe thread like braille, tremble when she tries to match a valve. She tells her crew she is just out of practice. She sleeps with the radio on, but only to static, because silence makes her aware of every breath. Today, she still works the northern suburbs' aging housing stock. She climbs into crawlspaces, but she measures the floorboards before stepping down, taps the walls twice, counts the air in the room. A gurgling drain makes her shoulders hike to her ears. She avoids clinics, telling herself she can read her own vitals, but she checks her pulse every hour, her thumb pressing hard enough to leave bruises. At night, her studio ceiling tiles warp into a hospital grid. She wakes dry-mouthed, fingers flexing as if unclenching invisible restraints. The dreams are not of the surgery; they are of the wait. The long, hollow stretches between heartbeats, between breaths, between being and nothing. She stops cooking elaborate meals, reducing her diet to bread and tea, wondering if swallowing is still safe. She walks past a hospital on her way to a job site and turns down the alley, breathing through her nose until the sirens fade. Her wrench slips in her palm. She does not pick it up immediately. She stands in the damp dark, waiting for her hands to remember what they used to know.
